To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we directly quantify by X-ray methods for the first time the selective accumulation of ions from the aquender the surface of glycolipids in Langmuir monomolayers at air-water interfaces, (ii) the observed selectivity depends on the structural motifs of the saccharides, and (iii) the selectivity is only observed in monolayers featuring a crystalline ordering of saccharide head-groups.
the interactions of saccharide surfaces with ions can be directly quantified and that the ion species attracted to the saccharide surfaces depends on the structural motifs of the saccharides.

we have directly measured the preferential accumulation, or selective binding, of ions from aqueous solutions at the surfaces of uncharged saccharides, and that we have shown that this selective binding is strongly dependent on the structural ordering of the sacchride surface, as determined by the saccharide's headgroup structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interactions between saccharides and ions in the context of glycolipids, which can be considered as model compounds for saccharides in biological and technical systems.
the interactions of ions with saccharide layers in the form of Langmuir monomolecular films at air/water interface and the resulting effects on the ion distribution at the interface.
the interactions of ions with saccharide surfaces and their consequences for the swelling and mechanical behavior of wood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the headgroup-ordered monolayers of uncharged glycolipids exhibit selective interactions with ions, which can have far-reaching implications in the fields of biology, biotechnology and materials science.
the headgroup ordering is a key parameter for ion-saccharide interactions.
the headgroup order in the lipid bilayer is the most important factor for the ion accumulation at the membrane interface.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have observed that saccharides can be selective for ions.
saccharide headgroup-ordered monolayers at the air/water interface can be used as a model system to investigate the selective interaction with ions in aqueous solution.
the saccharide surface can be used as a template to attract ions of specific charge.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structural ordering of the headgroups of uncharged saccharides is crucial for selective ion interactions.
the saccharide layer can act as an ion-specific gate to the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
saccharides can be used as a platform for selective ion adsorption.
